content:
Let  
\[
x=a+b,\quad y=b+c,\quad z=c+a.
\]
Then \(x+y+z=2n\), and
\[
xyz=(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)
\]
is a perfect cube. Also
\[
a=\frac{x+z-y}{2},\quad b=\frac{x+y-z}{2},\quad c=\frac{y+z-x}{2},
\]
so \(x,y,z\) must be distinct positive integers satisfying the triangle inequalities and \(x+y+z\) even.

For \(n<10\), we have \(x+y+z=2n<20\). Since \(a,b,c\) are distinct positive integers, \(n\ge 6\), so only \(n=6,7,8,9\) need checking.

The possible distinct triangle triples \((x,y,z)\) with even sum less than \(20\) are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
x+y+z & (x,y,z) & xyz\\
\hline
12 & (3,4,5) & 60\\
14 & (3,5,6) & 90\\
16 & (3,6,7),(4,5,7) & 126,140\\
18 & (3,7,8),(4,6,8),(5,6,7) & 168,192,210
\end{array}
\]
None of these products is a perfect cube. Hence no \(n<10\) works.

For \(n=10\), take
\[
a=1,\quad b=2,\quad c=7.
\]
Then
\[
a+b+c=10,
\]
and
\[
(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=3\cdot 8\cdot 9=216=6^3,
\]
which is a perfect cube.

Therefore, the smallest such natural number is
\[
\boxed{10}.
\]
